title: Opal and the Invisible Bracelet
subtitle: An invisible adventure helps Opal understand being apart.
editorialNote: New story adapted from a recovered plot summary; original wording was unavailable.

paragraphs: Opal found the bracelet beneath the last cushion in the galaxy tent. It was silver, with a clasp shaped like a tiny star. When she slipped it over her wrist, her hand disappeared.
Then her elbow disappeared. Then the rest of her.
Lolo looked up from the blanket. “Opal?”
“I'm here!”
“I know. You're standing on my corner.”
Opal stepped back. The blanket moved by itself. They both giggled.
Opal unfastened the bracelet and appeared again, curly hair first. “Do you think everyone would be all right if we went on a little adventure by ourselves?”
“Perhaps we could find out,” Lolo said. “But only for a little while. And we tell them afterward.”
Unique Pink helped make a pretend robot with a round cardboard head. Beside it they placed a folded blanket with a painted sloth face: a very unconvincing pretend Lolo.
Langston examined their work. “An excellent robot. Clearly based on my handsome features.”
“It has a cereal box for a face,” Opal said.
“An excellent cereal box.”
Opal wrote a note saying she and Lolo would be back soon. Then she tucked Lolo close, fastened the bracelet around them both, and stepped behind the tent flap.
At first the room carried on as usual. Cinny sorted ribbons. Coatl checked the cushion bridge. Finley opened her notebook while Stella sat beside the cardboard robot.
“Interesting,” Finley murmured.

illustration.alt: Opal holds her sloth lovey Lolo while reading inside the purple galaxy tent.

paragraphs: Axey bounced into the tent. He took one look at the pretend sloth and stopped bouncing.
“That Lolo has no paws.”
“Perhaps she's tucked them in,” Langston suggested.
“She also has a button drawn on her stomach.”
“A fashion decision.”
Axey leaned close to the robot. He knocked politely on its cereal-box head.
Clonk.
“Opal doesn't usually sound like breakfast.”
The stuffies gathered. Opal held very still behind the flap. She had expected everyone to keep playing. Instead, Cherryberry read the note carefully and asked Coatl to check that the paths were safe.
“We don't have to panic,” Cherryberry said. “But we can look out for our friends.”
The whole little group set off together. Even the plushies Opal thought would stay snuggled in bed came along. Axey carried Lolo's spare ribbon. Stella brought a blanket in case anyone got chilly.
Finley stopped at the doorway. On the dusty floor were two small footprints and a soft drag mark where Lolo's lovey blanket had brushed the ground.
“Three clues,” she announced.
Langston lifted his foot. “Four, if you count this magnificent one.”
“We don't.”
The trail led to the cushion garden, where the friends formed a patient search party. No one shouted. No one got lost. Coatl kept the smaller kitties together, while Cinny counted everyone twice.
Opal watched them helping one another. Something warm and uncomfortable curled inside her chest.
“They can manage,” she whispered. “But they're still worried.”
Lolo squeezed her hand. “Being able to manage doesn't mean you stop missing somebody.”
Opal unclasped the bracelet.
“There you are!” Axey cried. He bounced so high that he landed sitting down.
Opal knelt beside her friends. “I'm sorry. I wanted to see whether you'd be okay without me for a little while. I should have told you properly.”
Lolo stepped forward too. “I suggested trying it. We should have made a clear plan together.”
Cherryberry considered the bracelet. “A short adventure is fine. A mystery about where our friends have gone is harder.”
So they made a new plan: say where you are going, say when you will return, and ask who wants to come. Sometimes the answer could be everyone. Sometimes it could be just two friends.
“And sometimes,” Langston said, “it could be one extremely qualified robot.”
He put on the cereal box. It slipped over his eyes.
“ROBOT REQUESTS DIRECTIONS.”
Opal guided him gently away from the cushion pond. Lolo and Axey walked beside her, already planning a very visible expedition for tomorrow.
That evening the bracelet went into a small box beside the bed. The cardboard Lolo stayed outside it.
“She can guard the box,” Opal said.
“Very bravely,” Lolo agreed. “Without any paws.”
The End.
